claims.text: Heating AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles causes progressive phase separation and formation of an AuCu-enriched surface layer.
The AuCu surface layer melts at elevated temperature.
The segregated surface phase has a lower melting point than the nanoparticle core or corresponding bulk alloy.
Formation of the AuCu-rich surface phase locally weakens cohesive energy.
Melting of the segregated surface phase governs the overall premelting and melting behavior of the nanoparticles.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are equiatomic solid solutions with uniform elemental distributions at room temperature.
Reducing the Au concentration can suppress Au surface segregation.
Adding a chemically similar element that disfavors surface enrichment can suppress segregation.
The relevant thermal evolution of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles can be studied over approximately 298–973 K.
Pronounced atomic diffusion drives the temperature-dependent phase separation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Atomic diffusion in the quinary AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles is more active than in corresponding monometallic and bimetallic subsystems.
Differences in atomic size, bonding strength, and intrinsic melting point cause selected elements to migrate preferentially toward the nanoparticle surface.
Nanoparticles that permit segregation will develop surface disorder or melting at a lower temperature than compositionally modified nanoparticles with suppressed segregation.
Suppressing surface segregation will produce a higher and more spatially homogeneous melting temperature.
High-entropy nanoalloys generally contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallize as a solid solution.
The proposed mechanism should hold when at least one elemental pair has significantly different melting points and diffusion coefficients.
The mechanism may not apply when all constituent elements have nearly identical thermodynamic and kinetic properties.
